doc.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Vaudeville parents and early piano playing
summary: His parents were vaudevillians; his father became a San Diego Union editor, and Smith, an only child, took to the piano.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Were you forced into playing the piano or did it come—

No it was kind of fun. At the time, I don’t really remember how I started. I mean my folks tell me that I used to go over to the — they had a little ricca R-I-C-C-A piano. I’ve never seen one since. It was a good little upright. And my folks were in vaudeville. They were both very musical. My dad played trumpet and did comedy and my mom was a singer, and a very good one, judging from the press clipping they had in vaudeville, there are books of clippings and they’re all rave reviews so I guess they were very good. But they saw the handwriting on the wall when movies came in that vaudeville was going to be doomed and my dad being the brain that he was, he graduated from Boston Latin School in the east there, so you can go to any college that you want if you get out of Boston Latin School, they’ll love to have you. And he always wanted to be a newspaperman and write stories and all that. So he got a job on the San Diego Union as a cub reporter at about 15 bucks a week after having been in vaudeville making quite a lot more.

He finally became the Sunday editor of the paper, and bless their hearts they chose San Diego to settle down in to have children. And my mom had one giant child and then that’s all she could handle, that was me, I was an only child. I was almost ten pounds and my mother was five feet tall.
She used to say, “where did you come from?” My dad was six feet. But they tell me I went to the piano and rather than do this on it, I would play with the fingers. Not necessarily —
